items.stem: In MATLAB, what does the operator `.*` do between two equally sized matrices?

options.rationale: Correct: .* multiplies entries element by element.
Solving a system uses the backslash operator \.

items.explanation: Correct: .* multiplies entries element by element.

items.stem: Which statements about vectorisation in MATLAB are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Logical indexing can select elements that satisfy a condition without a loop
options.rationale: Correct: a logical mask indexes the array directly.

options.text: Vectorised array operations are typically faster than equivalent explicit loops
options.rationale: Correct: built-in array operations run in optimised native code.

options.text: Vectorisation requires the Parallel Computing Toolbox
options.rationale: Vectorisation is core MATLAB and needs no extra toolbox.

options.text: Element-wise operators require matrices of incompatible sizes
options.rationale: They require compatible sizes (or broadcastable ones).

items.explanation: Correct: a logical mask indexes the array directly.; Correct: built-in array operations run in optimised native code.

items.stem: Why is `A\b` generally preferred over `inv(A)*b` to solve `Ax=b`?

options.text: It is more numerically stable and usually faster
options.rationale: Correct: the backslash solver avoids forming the inverse, improving stability and speed.

options.text: It computes a different solution than the linear system
options.rationale: It solves the same system, just more reliably.

options.text: inv(A) does not exist in MATLAB
options.rationale: inv exists; it is simply the less stable choice here.

options.text: Backslash only works for diagonal matrices
options.rationale: Backslash handles general systems, not only diagonal ones.

items.explanation: Correct: the backslash solver avoids forming the inverse, improving stability and speed.
